extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of periodical essays, satire, and polite conversation (early-18th-century style)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for composing short periodical essays, satirical pieces, and letters (Spectator-style), and for conduct in conversation; includes tactics to interest readers and cautions about judgement and self‑exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include informative content
rubrics_metrics.description: Such Informations cannot but be highly improving to the Reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide information in essays that improves or enlightens the reader; pieces that supply useful facts or reflections are valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-reference unless character warrants it
rubrics_metrics.description: In Works of Humour, especially when a Man writes under a fictitious Personage, the talking of one's self may give some Diversion to the Publick; but I would advise every other Writer never to speak of himself, unless there be something very considerable in his Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use first‑person or autobiographical asides in humorous pieces or when the author's personal character is inherently interesting; otherwise refrain from speaking of oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present recycled jokes as your own
rubrics_metrics.description: Those empty conceited Fellows, who repeat as Sayings of their own... several Jests which were made before they were born... what he thought was a new Conceit... had appeared in Print before he or his ingenious Friends were ever heard of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming old or commonly known jests as original material; consult published jest-books and collections to check whether a conceit is genuinely new and prevent vapid egotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate an impartial spectator stance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the Work of a Philosopher to be every Day subduing his Passions, and laying aside his Prejudices. I endeavour at least to look upon Men and their Actions only as an impartial Spectator...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and commentators should moderate passions and prejudices, striving for an impartial view when judging persons and actions in essays or moral reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty, two-word judgments of character
rubrics_metrics.description: People... pronounce on every Man's Character, which they can give in two Words, and make him either good for nothing, or qualified for every thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that human character is complex; refrain from broad, absolute labels and acknowledge mixed virtues and vices in individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh circumstances before judging actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The very same Action may sometimes be so oddly circumstanced, that it is difficult to determine whether it ought to be rewarded or punish'd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating actions in essays or moral commentary, consider context and surrounding circumstances; an action's moral valence may shift with context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer public good over perfection in law and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: They have laid it down as one of their first Maxims, It is better suffering a Mischief than an Inconvenience; which is as much as to say... That since no Law can take in or provide for all Cases, it is better private Men should have some Injustice done them, than that a public Grievance should not be redressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing laws or policy, acknowledge the trade-off that perfect individual justice cannot always be achieved without harming the common good; use this principle to temper critiques of legal systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical or exemplary anecdotes to illustrate moral complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall close my Paper for this Day [with Plutarch's Spartan example]... The Gallantry of this Action was judged so great... they decreed he should be presented with a Garland; but... fined him a thousand Drachmas for going out to the Battle unarmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ well-chosen historical stories to show tension between valor and rule-following or to exemplify nuanced moral lessons; juxtapose praise with censure to provoke reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military experience as a source of civic virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The Army not only gives a Man Opportunities of exercising those two great Virtues Patience and Courage, but often produces them in Minds where they had scarce any Footing before...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing character sketches or persuasive letters, consider citing military service as formative of patience, courage, social ease, and certain practical virtues—while acknowledging possible negative 'military airs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical omission and innuendo to engage readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A sprinkling of the Words Faction, Frenchman, Papist, Plunderer... An M and an h, a T and an r, with a short Line between them... our Party-writers... never mention the Q--n or P--l at length, though they speak of them with Honour... It gives a secret Satisfaction to a Peruser of these mysterious Works, that he is able to decipher them without help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate partial suppression of names (dashes, asterisks, omitted vowels) and use of innuendo creates reader involvement and curiosity; it can make political or scandalous writing more enticing and appear 'safer' while still implying targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ provocative catchwords and italics to attract purchasers
rubrics_metrics.description: A sprinkling of the Words Faction, Frenchman, Papist, Plunderer, and the like significant Terms, in an Italick Character, have also a very good Effect upon the Eye of the Purchaser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To increase the marketability of pamphlets or papers, use striking topical words and typographic emphasis to catch readers' attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use puzzles/enigmas and partial publication to stimulate readership
rubrics_metrics.description: I have here drawn up a very curious Libel... I shall leave this with my curious Reader, as some ingenious Writers do their Enigmas, and if any sagacious Person can fairly unriddle it, I will print his Explanation...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering partial texts or enigmas and inviting reader solutions encourages engagement and repeat readership; withholding material can be an editorial device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious: omission can please but still provoke dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: He [a reader] observed the SPECTATOR is very cautious of giving Offence, and has therefore put two Dashes into his Pudding... the furious Statesman... Why does not he write it at length, if he means honestly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While dashes/asterisks can mitigate direct offence, they do not eliminate political sensitivity; anticipate debate and strong reactions from readers with opposing views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphorical military tactics in social/courtship advice (rhetorical device)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether I had best Storm or proceed by way of Sap... I made a Lodgment in an outer Parlour... I intend to insist upon Carte-Blanche, and am in hopes, by keeping off all other Pretenders for the Space of twenty four Hours, to starve her into a Compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying siege/campaign metaphors (storm, sap, blockade) is an effective rhetorical strategy in letters and essays about pursuit or persuasion; adapt the tactic metaphor to the social situation but beware of absurd literalism.
